title: European Soccer Nations Threaten World Cup Boycott Over Fifa's Privatization Plan
summary: What would you do if someone tried to sell your most cherished tradition to the highest bidder? For Europe's soccer nations, the answer is clear: walk away. In an unprecedented show of unity, all 55 member associations of Uefa voted Thursday to boycott all Fifa competitions — including the men's and women's World Cups — if Fifa proceeds with a controversial plan to sell ownership stakes to private investors. The decision came during an emergency virtual meeting chaired by Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin, following a proposal announced earlier this week by Fifa president Gianni Infantino. The atmosphere was described as 'venomous,' with FA chairwoman Debbie Hewitt and CEO Mark Bullingham among the vocal critics. Hewitt, despite being one of eight Fifa vice-presidents, had no prior knowledge of Infantino's discussions. At the heart of the dispute is Infantino's plan to create a commercial subsidiary, Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE), to manage flagship events. External investors would be invited to make 'minority, non-controlling investments.' Infantino has dangled a $40 million carrot before Fifa's 211 member associations, setting a September 19 deadline for approval to access an initial $20 million. The lead investor group is expected to be Thrive Eternal, a venture capital firm founded by Joshua Kushner — brother of Jared Kushner, son-in-law of former U.S. President Donald Trump. The White House has declined to comment. Uefa's statement was unequivocal: 'We unanimously and unequivocally reject Fifa's proposal to transfer ownership interests in the World Cup and other Fifa competitions to private investors.' They added, 'The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product. It is one of football's greatest sporting legacies... No part of it should ever be surrendered to private investors.' The boycott threat, if triggered, would first be tested at the Women's World Cup play-offs in October. For a sport already grappling with issues of commercialization, this standoff could redefine who truly owns the beautiful game.
why_it_matters: This power struggle decides who controls the world's most popular sport. If private investors buy into the World Cup, they could push for changes that prioritize profit—like moving games to richer countries or raising ticket and TV prices—which would affect young fans and future generations of players.

background_read: FIFA (Fédération Internationale de Football Association) is the global organization that oversees soccer and runs the World Cup, a tournament watched by billions. UEFA (Union of European Football Associations) governs soccer in Europe and has often clashed with FIFA over control.

The World Cup has never been sold to outside investors before; this proposal marks a radical change in sports governance. Private investment firms often buy parts of companies to earn future profits, but selling a piece of a cultural event like the World Cup raises big questions.

Thrive Eternal, the investment group mentioned, was founded by Joshua Kushner—the brother of Jared Kushner, who was a senior advisor to former U.S. President Donald Trump. This family connection adds political tension to the business deal.

Boycotts in sports are rare but have happened before, such as countries refusing to attend the 1980 Moscow Olympics over political disagreements. If European teams walk away, the World Cup would lose its most famous teams and huge TV audiences.
Article_Structure: LEAD: A rhetorical question about selling a cherished tradition, answered by Europe's defiance.
KEY EVENT: All 55 UEFA associations vote to boycott FIFA events if privatization goes ahead, in an 'unprecedented' and 'venomous' meeting.
├─ WHO: UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin chaired the meeting; FA chairwoman Debbie Hewitt and CEO Mark Bullingham were vocal critics.
└─ WHAT: The proposal—a commercial subsidiary (FFE) to let private investors own a minority stake in the World Cup and other tournaments.
MONEY AND DEADLINE: FIFA president Gianni Infantino offers each of 211 member associations $40 million total, with $20 million up front if they approve by September 19.
└─ THE INVESTOR: Thrive Eternal, a venture capital firm led by Joshua Kushner, brother of Jared Kushner (son-in-law of ex-President Trump). The White House won't comment.
TENSION / REACTION: UEFA's statement rejects the plan 'unanimously and unequivocally,' declaring the World Cup a legacy that should never be sold as an investment product.
OPEN QUESTION: Will the boycott actually happen? The first test could come at the Women's World Cup play-offs in October, which could reshape who owns the 'beautiful game.'

perspectives.perspective: Positive: Financial boost for soccer development
perspectives.description: Supporters argue that private investment could bring much-needed money to grow the sport in poorer nations and improve infrastructure. FIFA would still hold majority control, so the game's integrity remains protected while new funds accelerate global development.

perspectives.perspective: Negative: Selling out a cultural heritage
perspectives.description: Critics see this as a betrayal of the sport's soul. Once the World Cup becomes a commercial product, decisions could be driven by profits rather than fairness. The threat by European federations shows how strongly many inside football reject treating the tournament like a business to be carved up.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral: Part of a long-term trend
perspectives.description: This clash is the latest chapter in a decades-long story of sports commercialisation. From shirt sponsorships to billion-dollar TV deals, outside money has shaped football for years. The FIFA plan pushes the boundary even further, testing how far fans and nations will accept market logic in a traditionally communal game.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking: Possibility of a split in world football
perspectives.description: If UEFA carries out its boycott, the World Cup's value and legitimacy would collapse, possibly forcing FIFA to back down. In the longer term, this could lead to a permanent split, with European nations organising their own global tournament outside FIFA's control—something that would fundamentally redraw the map of international sport.
